kernels.l1: Sometimes one sentence is really two promises. You have to keep them both.
kernels.l2: An "exactly when" telling is two promises hiding in one sentence. To show it is kept, check both boxes — one promise each way.
kernels.l3: "A if and only if B" means both if–then claims at once: if A then B, and if B then A. To prove it you must check both boxes, writing one proof for each direction.
kernels.l4: p ⇔ q abbreviates (p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p). Proving a biconditional means writing two proofs, and either direction may be done by contrapositive.
kernels.l5: A biconditional p ⇔ q asserts that p and q are true in exactly the same cases; establishing it requires proving both implications separately.
kernels.l6: p ⇔ q holds exactly when p and q have identical truth values; proof requires both directions, and definitions are almost always biconditionals in disguise.
kernels.l7: The biconditional p ⇔ q is the conjunction of p ⇒ q and its converse; proving it means supplying two independent proofs, and each direction may need a different technique.
kernels.l8: p ⇔ q asserts logical equivalence inside the object language; iff-chains are legitimate only when every link is genuinely reversible, and definitions are stipulative biconditionals.
